figures.caption: The same five people in two different teams. The attribute table is identical; the pattern of ties is not, and neither is what happens when Ana has a bad week.
figures.alt: Two network diagrams of the same five people. On the left every person is connected to every other person. On the right, Ana is in the center connected to the four others, who are not connected to each other.

figures.caption: The rhythm of every measure in the book: start from the idea, be clear about the data, compute, interpret, doubt, and loop back.
figures.alt: A left-to-right flow of five labeled boxes: Idea, Data, Compute, Interpret, Doubt. A dashed arrow runs from the last box back to the first.

figures.caption: Simmel's contrast. A pair depends on both members. Add a third person and new roles appear, such as the one in the middle.
figures.alt: Left: two nodes joined by a line. Middle: three nodes joined in a triangle. Right: three nodes where the middle node is joined to both others, and a dashed line shows no direct tie between those two.

figures.caption: Heider's balance rule on four triangles. Multiply the three signs: a positive product is balanced. Line style and symbol repeat the colors, so the figure reads in greyscale.
figures.alt: Four triangles with signed ties. Plus, plus, plus: balanced. One plus and two minus: balanced. Two plus and one minus: unbalanced. Three minus: unbalanced.

figures.caption: Cartwright and Harary's result: a signed network is balanced exactly when it can be split into two camps, friendly inside and hostile between.
figures.alt: Five nodes in two outlined groups. The three nodes of Camp 1 are joined by positive ties, the two nodes of Camp 2 by one positive tie, and three negative dashed ties cross between the camps.

figures.caption: Granovetter's bridge. Within each circle everyone is tied to everyone, so information circulates but is mostly redundant; the single weak tie is the route for new information.
figures.alt: Two outlined clusters, each with four fully connected nodes drawn with thick gray lines. A single dashed orange line links one orange node in the left cluster to one orange node in the right cluster.

figures.caption: Both egos have four contacts. On the left the contacts are all tied to each other (closure). On the right ego is the only link between two groups (a structural hole).
figures.alt: Two diagrams of an orange node with four contacts. On the left the four contacts are connected to each other. On the right the contacts form two separate pairs with no ties between the pairs.

data.right: ego with 2 pairs of contacts, no tie between pairs

figures.caption: Homophily in one picture. The same ten people and the same two groups; what changes is where the ties go. To claim a preference, compare against what group sizes alone would produce.
figures.alt: Two network diagrams of ten people, five circles and five squares. In the left diagram seven of nine ties cross between the shapes. In the right diagram only one of thirteen ties crosses.

figures.caption: The small-world effect. Both rings are equally clustered; adding three long-range shortcuts cuts the average distance between people noticeably.
figures.alt: Two circular networks of sixteen nodes. The right one has three extra straight orange lines crossing the circle. Captions give the average distance in each.

figures.caption: The same five-person advice network in the three standard formats. They hold the same information; they differ in what they are good at.
figures.alt: A directed network of five people shown as a picture, with the same ties as a five by five matrix of ones and zeros, as a seven-row edge list, and as a list of who each person goes to.

figures.caption: Two-mode data (people and events) and its one-mode projection (people tied by shared events), after the idea of the duality of persons and groups.
figures.alt: Left: people P1 to P4 each linked to events E1 to E3. Right: a chain of people P2, P1, P3, P4 where each neighboring pair is tied and the tie is labeled with the event they share.

figures.caption: Boundary choices change results. Nodes near the cut lose ties to people outside the data, so their measures understate how connected they are.
figures.alt: A network inside a dashed outline. Two orange nodes on its right edge have dashed red ties leading out to three gray nodes outside the outline, which are not part of the data.

figures.caption: Levels of analysis on one network. Each question lives at one level; a statement about a node is not a statement about the whole network.
figures.alt: Five copies of the same seven-node network. Each highlights something different in orange: a single node, a pair of tied nodes, a triangle, a five-node cluster, and finally the whole network in blue.

figures.caption: One network, three pictures. Nothing about the data changed; only the positions did. Only the last layout lets the three groups show.
figures.alt: Three drawings of the same eighteen nodes, which belong to three groups drawn as circles, squares and diamonds. In the first, positions are random and ties form a tangle. In the second, nodes sit on a circle and many ties cross the middle. In the third, each group forms its own tight cluster with a few ties between the clusters.

figures.caption: Distance on the page can mislead. A stress layout tries to make distance on the page match steps in the network; a circle ignores it.
figures.alt: Left: a circular drawing of an eighteen-node network with two nodes ringed in red that sit next to each other on the circle, joined by a dashed red line. Right: a stress-layout drawing of the same network with the same two nodes ringed in red, now far apart.

figures.caption: The same network twice. When a node-link drawing turns into a hairball, a matrix with rows sorted by group shows the block structure immediately.
figures.alt: Left: a tangled circular drawing of twenty-four nodes in three groups. Right: a twenty-four by twenty-four grid of squares, with three dense blocks along the diagonal outlined in black and very few filled squares outside them.

figures.caption: Four visual channels and what each can carry. Pick one idea per channel and say what it is in a legend.
figures.alt: A ten-node network drawn in two clusters. Larger nodes have more ties. Circles and squares in different colors mark the two groups. Thicker lines mark stronger ties. A list on the right names each channel and what it encodes.

figures.caption: One network, four rankings. Each measure answers a different question, so each picks a different person as most central.
figures.alt: Four copies of the same ten-node network. In the degree and eigenvector panels the node Dev, near the middle of the left cluster, is the largest. In the closeness panel two nodes, Fay and Gus, are largest and equal. In the betweenness panel Hana, on the narrow link leading out to two more people, is largest.

figures.caption: Betweenness is about routes. Every shortest route from Jo to anyone else passes through Ivo and Hana, so they sit in between even though neither has many ties.
figures.alt: A ten-node network. Thick orange lines mark the shortest routes starting at the node Jo: Jo to Ivo, Ivo to Hana, then Hana to the two nodes Fay and Gus, and on from them to the rest. Thin gray lines mark ties not on those routes.

figures.caption: Centralization summarizes a whole network: how far the most central person stands above everyone else, compared with the most extreme case.
figures.alt: Three ten-node networks side by side. A star with one hub joined to nine others is labeled 1.00. The friendship network with one slightly larger hub is labeled 0.33. A ring in which everyone has two ties is labeled 0.00.

figures.caption: In a directed network, activity (going to others) and prestige (being gone to) are different things. Chloe is sought out by everyone and seeks out one person; Dev and Eli seek out others but nobody seeks them.
figures.alt: A grouped bar chart for Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev and Eli. Out-degree bars are solid blue: 2, 1, 1, 2, 1. In-degree bars are dashed orange: 2, 1, 4, 0, 0. Chloe's in-degree bar is the tallest.

figures.caption: Three kinds of route from Ana to Eli. A walk may repeat anything; a path never repeats a person; a shortest path (a geodesic) uses the fewest steps. Distance is the length of a shortest path.
figures.alt: Three drawings of a five-person network in which Ben, Cleo and Dev form a triangle, Ana hangs off Ben and Eli hangs off Dev. Left: a walk from Ana to Eli that goes to Cleo and back to Ben, five steps. Middle: a path through Ben, Cleo and Dev, four steps. Right: a shortest path through Ben and Dev, three steps.

figures.caption: The distance table for the friendship network. Its largest entry is the diameter; its average over pairs is the mean distance; each row's largest entry is that person's eccentricity.
figures.alt: A ten by ten grid of numbers. The diagonal is zero. Most entries are 1, 2 or 3. The darkest entries, 4, appear between Jo and each of the first five people in the list. A column at the right gives each person's largest distance.

figures.caption: Density is the share of possible ties that are present. With six people there are 15 possible ties.
figures.alt: Three drawings of six people on a circle. A path of five ties has density 0.33. A ring with three crossing ties, nine in all, has density 0.60. All fifteen ties give density 1.00.

figures.caption: Local clustering for the person in the middle: of all pairs of their friends, what share are friends with each other?
figures.alt: Three drawings of a person in the middle tied to four friends. In the first no two friends are tied, giving 0 of 6, clustering 0.00. In the second two pairs of friends are tied, 2 of 6, clustering 0.33. In the third all pairs are tied, 6 of 6, clustering 1.00.

figures.caption: Components. In an undirected network a component is a piece in which everyone can reach everyone. In a directed network we distinguish weak components (ignore arrow direction) from strong ones (follow the arrows both ways).
figures.alt: Left: a four-person cluster and a separate three-person triangle, with no tie between them. Right: three people joined in a one-way cycle and two people who point at each other, with one dashed arrow from the cycle to the pair.

figures.caption: k-cores. A person's core number is the largest k for which they belong to a group where everyone has at least k ties inside the group. Seven people are in the 3-core.
figures.alt: The ten-person friendship network. Seven nodes drawn as blue circles form the dense cluster. Hana, drawn as an orange square, hangs off it. Ivo and Jo, drawn as purple diamonds, trail off at the far end.

figures.caption: All sixteen triad types. In each triangle the same three people appear in the same places; only the ties differ. The code reads as the number of mutual pairs, asymmetric pairs and empty pairs, with a letter for the finer shape.
figures.alt: A four by four grid of sixteen small directed triangles, each with its code and description. Row one: 003 no ties, 012 one tie, 102 one mutual pair, 021D one person sends to two. Row two: 021U two send to one, 021C a chain, 111D a mutual pair with one more pointing at it, 111U a mutual pair that points at one more. Row three: 030T a transitive pecking order, 030C a cycle, 201 two mutual pairs, 120D a mutual pair where one sends to both. Row four: 120U a mutual pair where both send to one, 120C a mutual pair with a chain, 210 two mutual pairs and one more tie, 300 everyone mutual.

figures.caption: An office advice network. Shape and color mark the position: leaders (diamonds), managers (squares) and staff (circles). Nobody in the bottom row asks anybody else in the bottom row, and yet they have a lot in common.
figures.alt: Ten people in three rows. Two leaders at the top, Ada and Ben, point at each other. Three managers in the middle each point at both leaders. Five staff at the bottom each point at one manager: Flo and Gus at Cy, Hal at Dee, and Ivy and Jay at Eve.

figures.caption: Structural equivalence asks for the same ties to the same people. Regular equivalence asks only for the same kinds of ties to people who are themselves alike. Flo and Gus are both; Flo and Hal are only the second.
figures.alt: Two small drawings. In each, Ada at the top receives from two managers, Cy and Dee, and three staff members each point at a manager. On the left, Flo and Gus are highlighted and both point at Cy. On the right, Flo and Hal are highlighted: Flo points at Cy and Hal points at Dee.

figures.caption: A blockmodel squeezes the matrix of who goes to whom into one number per pair of positions (the density of that block) and then into a 1 or a 0 (the image). Here three positions and three ones tell the whole story.
figures.alt: On the left, a ten by ten grid with blue cells where a person asks another for advice, separated by heavy lines into leaders, managers and staff. Blue cells fill the leaders' own block and the managers-to-leaders block, and a scatter in the staff-to-managers block. On the right, a three by three table of block densities with values 1.00 for leaders to leaders and managers to leaders, 0.33 for staff to managers and 0 elsewhere, and below it the image matrix with ones in those three places.

figures.caption: The discrete core-periphery model. Split people into a core and a periphery and compare the network with an ideal pattern: the core is tied to itself, the periphery is not, and core-to-periphery pairs are left out. The best split is the one whose pattern fits the real ties best.
figures.alt: On the left, the ten-person friendship network with five people drawn as blue circles in the dense middle and five drawn as orange squares around the edge. On the right, a ten by ten grid ordered core first: the upper-left five by five block is blue, the lower-right block is white, and the two off-diagonal blocks are gray.

figures.caption: An ego network is a person, their contacts, and the ties among those contacts. Dev's contacts mostly know each other. Hana's mostly do not, so Hana links people who would otherwise be apart.
figures.alt: Two drawings. On the left, Dev, an orange square in the middle, with six contacts in a hexagon around them, joined in a ring by blue ties with two extra blue ties across the ring. On the right, Hana, an orange square, with three contacts: Fay and Gus are joined to each other by a blue tie, and Ivo is not tied to either.

figures.caption: Effective size counts a person's contacts, minus the redundancy among them. Three contacts who all know each other add up to one contact's worth of access. Three who do not add up to three.
figures.alt: Two drawings of a person at the center with three contacts around them. On the left the three contacts are joined to one another by blue ties, a triangle, and the effective size is 1. On the right the three contacts have no ties among themselves and the effective size is 3.

figures.caption: Effective size and constraint for the friendship network. Dev has the largest effective size, but Hana has the lowest constraint: she is the only person whose contacts live in different parts of the network.
figures.alt: Two horizontal bar charts with the same ten names. Effective size: Dev 3.33, Fay and Gus 3.00, Hana 2.33, Ana and Ben 2.00, Ivo 2.00, Cleo, Eli and Jo 1.00. Constraint: Hana is lowest at 0.43, then Fay and Gus at 0.45, Dev 0.47, Ivo 0.50, Ana and Ben 0.54, Cleo and Eli 0.66, Jo 1.00. Hana's bars are highlighted in orange.

figures.caption: Gould and Fernandez's five brokerage roles. The same chain of two arrows, i to j to k, is a different role depending on which groups the three people belong to. Person j is the broker.
figures.alt: Five panels, each showing three people i, j and k in a row joined by two arrows. Coordinator: all three are blue circles. Itinerant: i and k are blue circles and j is an orange square. Representative: i and j are blue circles and k is an orange square. Gatekeeper: i is a blue circle, j and k are orange squares. Liaison: i is a blue circle, j an orange square and k a purple diamond.

figures.caption: The E-I index for each person is (external ties minus internal ties) divided by all their ties. It runs from -1 (all ties inside the group) to +1 (all ties outside it). Here the groups are the first five people and the other five.
figures.alt: Ten horizontal bars, one per person, each made of blocks: blue blocks for ties to their own group and orange blocks for ties to the other group. Fay and Gus have three orange blocks and two blue, giving E-I of plus 0.20. Hana, Ivo and Jo have only blue blocks, giving minus 1.00. Ana and Ben have one orange block and three blue, giving minus 0.50.

figures.caption: The QAP reference distribution: the correlation between friendship and sharing a floor after relabeling the people 10,000 times, with the observed value marked. Relabeled correlations center near zero, and the observed value sits in the right tail.
figures.alt: A bar chart of 10,000 relabeled correlations, which take only a handful of distinct values, centered near zero and spread from about minus 0.3 to plus 0.4. A vertical black line marks the observed correlation, 0.365, in the right tail, where the bars are drawn in orange. A dashed gray curve shows the normal spread an ordinary test would assume.

figures.caption: Common ERGM statistics. Each panel shows the pattern that is counted. Shared partners are the people two tied nodes both know.
figures.alt: Six small drawings of network patterns. Edges: two nodes joined by a line. Same side: two circles joined by a line, which counts, and a circle and a square joined by a dashed line, which does not. Two-star: one node joined to two others. Triangle: three nodes all joined. Shared partners: two tied nodes, drawn in orange, with three common neighbors between them, and a note that each extra shared partner counts less. Hub: one node joined to six others.

figures.caption: How well each model reproduces features of the karate club it was not fit to. Each dot is the average over simulated networks as a percent of the real count, so 100 means a perfect match.
figures.alt: A dot chart with three rows: triangles, two-stars and three-stars. For triangles, the edges-and-side model is at 48 percent and the model with shared partners at 94 percent. For two-stars, the dots are at 65 and 74 percent. For three-stars, they are at 27 and 38 percent. A vertical line marks 100 percent.

figures.caption: A two-dimensional latent space fitted to the karate club. Nearby members are more likely to be friends. Members 4 and 10, and 5 and 6, land on exactly the same spot, so each pair shows as one marker. The axes have no meaning, and the map could be rotated or flipped.
figures.alt: A scatter of 34 markers joined by light grey lines for the 78 friendships. Blue circles for Mr. Hi's side sit mostly in the right and upper right, with Mr. Hi near the middle. Orange squares for the officer's side sit mostly on the left, with the officer toward the left center. A few members of each side are mixed in near the center.

figures.caption: The karate club's adjacency matrix, with members ordered two ways. Each blue cell is a friendship. Left: grouped by the side each member took, which gives two blocks of similar density. Right: grouped by the five most connected members (0, 1, 2, 32 and 33) and everyone else, the grouping the block model prefers.
figures.alt: Two 34 by 34 grids of cells, blue where two members are friends. The left grid is split into two equal halves by heavy lines, with blue cells concentrated in the two diagonal blocks and few in the off-diagonal blocks. The right grid is split after the first five rows and columns. Its small top-left block and its top and left strips are dense, and the large lower-right block is sparse.

figures.caption: The description length of three groupings of the karate club, split into its parts. Splitting into the club's two sides makes the network cheaper to describe but costs more to describe the groups and their ties, so the total gets worse. The hubs-and-the-rest grouping wins.
figures.alt: Three horizontal stacked bars. One group: 231.1 for the network given the groups, 3.5 for the groups, total 234.7. The club's two sides: 204.3, 28.6 and 8.1, total 241.0. Hubs and the rest: 187.7, 19.6 and 8.1, total 215.3.

figures.caption: The same six contacts, drawn as a timeline. Left: Ana reaches Ben at time 1 and Cleo at time 3, then runs out of later contacts. Right: Dev reaches everyone, because the contacts arrive in a useful order. A network drawn without time would make all six people equally connected.
figures.alt: Two timelines side by side, with six horizontal lines for Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli and Fay and vertical bars for six contacts at times 1 to 6. On the left, only the contacts at times 1 (Ana and Ben) and 3 (Ben and Cleo) are highlighted. On the right, all six contacts are highlighted and each person is labeled with the time Dev's message reaches them: Cleo 2, Ben 3, Eli 4, Ana 5, Fay 6.

figures.caption: Burstiness B compares the spread of the waiting times between events with their average. Evenly spaced events have B of -1. Events that arrive in clumps with long silences between have B above 0.
figures.alt: Two rows of vertical tick marks across a timeline. The top row, labeled a metronome with B of minus 1, has ticks at equal spacing. The bottom row, labeled the message stream with B of 0.27, has 80 ticks gathered into clumps separated by long empty stretches.

figures.caption: Simulating one period of the office advice network (@sec-positions-and-roles) forward from its starting point, 2,000 times for each setting. Left: ties thin out either way because the outdegree coefficient is negative. Right: with a positive reciprocity coefficient, the ties that survive are much more often mutual.
figures.alt: Two groups of three bars. In the Ties group, the start has 13 ties, the run without reciprocity averages 5.78 and the run with reciprocity 1.5 averages 7.33. In the Mutual pairs group, the start has 1, the run without reciprocity 0.18, and the run with reciprocity 1.17.

figures.caption: Davis, Gardner and Gardner's southern women [@davis1941deep]. Left: the incidence matrix, one blue cell for every attendance (89 in all). Right: its projection onto the women, where each cell counts the events a pair shared. The two groups of women show up as two dense blocks, with a thin bridge between them.
figures.alt: Two grids. The left grid has 18 rows for women and 14 columns for events, with 89 blue cells. Blue cells form a band that runs from the upper left, where the first women attended events 1 to 9, to the lower right, where the last women attended events 7 to 14. The right grid has 18 rows and 18 columns shaded by the number of shared events from 0 to 7. Dark shading fills the top-left block of the first nine women and the bottom-right block of the last nine, with lighter shading elsewhere.

figures.caption: Attendance at each of the fourteen events (bars) and the number of pairs of women each one ties together when the data are projected onto the women (the row beneath). A pair count grows with the square of the attendance, so the two biggest events account for almost half of all the shared-event counts.
figures.alt: A bar chart of 14 events. Attendance is 3, 3, 6, 4, 8, 8, 10, 14, 12, 5, 4, 6, 3 and 3. Beneath each bar is the number of pairs the event ties: 3, 3, 15, 6, 28, 28, 45, 91, 66, 10, 6, 15, 3, 3. Events 8 and 9, with 14 and 12 attendees, are highlighted.

figures.caption: Zachary's karate club. Shape shows who sided with whom when the club split; color shows the four communities found by Louvain. The communities refine the split rather than contradicting it.
figures.alt: A network of 34 people. Circles are members who stayed with the instructor and squares followed the administrator. Four colors mark communities: two colors cover almost only circles, two cover almost only squares, with one circle among the squares' communities and one square among the circles' communities.

figures.caption: Modularity adds up, over communities, how much more of the network's ties fall inside the community than random rewiring would put there. Here the four communities sum to Q = 0.419.
figures.alt: A grouped bar chart with four pairs of bars, one pair per community. In every pair the solid bar, the observed share of ties inside the community, is taller than the dashed bar, the share expected by chance.

figures.caption: The resolution setting controls how fine the communities are. The setting with the highest modularity is not necessarily the one that matches your question.
figures.alt: A bar chart with five bars for resolution settings 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 3, showing 2, 4, 5, 8 and 12 communities. The bar for resolution 1, four communities, is highlighted because it has the highest modularity, 0.419.

figures.caption: Subgroup definitions run from strict to loose. A clique allows no missing ties; a near-clique allows a few; a community only asks for more ties inside than you would expect by chance.
figures.alt: Left: five people on a circle with every pair tied. Middle: five people on a circle with two dashed red lines marking the two missing ties, so each person is missing at most one. Right: two small clusters of four, blue circles and orange squares, joined by a single tie.

figures.caption: Fifteen leading families of Florence around 1430. A line means a marriage joined the two families. The Medici are in orange.
figures.alt: A network of fifteen labeled dots joined by twenty lines. The Medici, drawn in orange, sit in the middle with six lines. A few families such as Pazzi and Salviati hang off the edge with only one or two lines.

figures.caption: The same marriage network with each family sized by betweenness. The Medici are far larger than anyone else: about half of all shortest routes between families go through them.
figures.alt: The fifteen-family marriage network again, now with dots of different sizes. The Medici dot in the middle is by far the largest and labeled 47.5. Guadagni, Albizzi and Salviati are medium sized and labeled. The families at the edge are tiny.

figures.caption: Krackhardt's 21 managers, three kinds of ties. Dot size shows how many people name that manager. The filled dot is the CEO (level 1).
figures.alt: Three copies of the same 21 dots. The left copy has many arrows, the middle fewer, the right is a tree of reporting lines with the filled CEO dot at the top. Manager 2 is the largest dot in the advice and friendship copies; manager 14 is the largest in the reporting copy.

figures.caption: Closeness for Jo, drawn. Each person is labeled with their distance from Jo; darker means farther. The distances sum to 29, so closeness is 9 / 29 = 0.310.
figures.alt: The ten-person network. Jo is on the right edge in blue. Each other person shows a number from 1 to 5, the number of steps to Jo, and is shaded darker as the number grows. A side note adds the distances to 29 and gives 9 divided by 29 as 0.310.

figures.caption: Eigenvector centrality as a passing game. Everyone starts at 1; each round, a person's new score is the sum of their neighbors' scores, rescaled so the top is 1. The scores settle: C is the best connected, D the least.
figures.alt: Four copies of a triangle A, B, C with a tail D attached to C. Dots grow or shrink with scores written beneath. At the start all are 1. After two rounds C is 1, A and B are 1, D is 0.6. Settled, C is 1.00, A and B 0.85 and D 0.46.

figures.caption: The Medici's betweenness (47.5) against 1,000 random marriage networks in which every family keeps its number of marriages. The real value sits in the upper part of the spread but not beyond it. The draws behind this picture are not the ones in the code, so counts differ slightly.
figures.alt: A histogram of the Medici's betweenness across 1,000 random networks, rising from near zero to a peak around 40 and falling off by about 65. A black vertical line marks the real value, 47.5. Bars from the 45 to 50 bin onward are orange. In these draws 199 of 1,000 reach the real value; the average is 39.6.

figures.caption: Leave out each of the twenty marriages in turn. In every case the Medici (orange) still have more betweenness than the best other family (blue), but the gap shrinks to a few points when the Albizzi–Medici marriage is left out.
figures.alt: Twenty rows, one per marriage left out, sorted from lowest Medici betweenness at the top (23.5) to highest at the bottom (57.5). In every row an orange dot for the Medici lies to the right of a blue dot for the best other family. A dashed vertical line marks the Medici's value with all marriages, 47.5. The two dots are closest in the row for the Albizzi–Medici marriage.

figures.caption: The southern women as a two-mode network: 18 women on the left, 14 events on the right, one line for each of the 89 attendances. Every line runs between the two columns, never within one. The lines of event 8, the biggest, are orange.
figures.alt: Eighteen women in a left column and fourteen events in a right column, joined by 89 lines. Event 8 has 14 lines, drawn in orange, and event 9 has 12. The first women connect mostly to events 1 to 9 and the last women mostly to events 7 to 14. No line joins two women or two events.

figures.caption: The incidence matrix as a picture. A blue cell means the woman (row) attended the event (column). The numbers on the right are row totals, the number of events each woman attended; the numbers underneath are column totals, the number of women at each event.
figures.alt: A grid of 18 rows, one for each woman, and 14 columns, one for each event, with 89 blue cells. Row totals on the right run from 2 to 8. Column totals underneath are 3, 3, 6, 4, 8, 8, 10, 14, 12, 5, 4, 6, 3, 3, with the 14 and the 12 for events 8 and 9 in orange. Blue cells run in a band from the upper left to the lower right.

figures.caption: The projection onto the women, drawn two ways. Left: every pair that shared at least one event, 139 of the 153 possible pairs, a hairball. Right: only the 24 pairs that shared four or more events, where two groups of women (the first nine listed, in blue, and the last nine, in orange) become visible: none of the strong ties crosses between them.
figures.alt: Two rings of the same 18 women, with the first nine in blue and the last nine in orange. The left ring has 139 gray lines, so many that individual ties cannot be told apart. The right ring has 24 blue lines, thicker for pairs that shared more events, and every one of them joins two women of the same color. Four women, Dorothy, Olive, Flora and Pearl, have no line.

figures.caption: Each dot is one of the 139 pairs of women who shared at least one event, plotted by plain count (across) and Newman weight (up). Pairs with the same count can have very different Newman weights, because small events count for more. The strongest pair under each weighting is orange.
figures.alt: A scatter plot of 139 dots. The horizontal axis is shared events from 0 to 7 and the vertical axis is Newman weight from 0 to 2. Dots with the same count are spread vertically: pairs with 3 shared events have Newman weights from 0.28 to 0.68. Two dots are orange and labeled: Evelyn and Theresa at 7 shared events, and Sylvia and Nora with the highest Newman weight.

figures.caption: An invented example of a hairball. Eight people share four small events (choir, chess, quiz, garden) and one town hall that all of them attended. With the town hall, every one of the 28 pairs is tied. Without it, eight pairs remain, in two clusters.
figures.alt: Two rings of the same eight people, Ana to Hana, invented for illustration. The left ring has 28 lines, one for every pair. The right ring has 8 blue lines forming two separate clusters: Ana, Ben, Cleo and Dev in one, Esi, Finn, Gus and Hana in the other.

figures.caption: Krackhardt's 21 managers drawn three times with every manager in the same place each time. Lines show a tie in either direction. Manager 2 (blue) and manager 17 (orange) are marked so you can follow them from layer to layer.
figures.alt: Three copies of the same 21 dots in the same positions. The left copy, advice, has 145 lines and is dense. The middle copy, friendship, has 79 lines. The right copy, reporting lines, has 20 lines and forms a tree. Two dots are larger and filled in every copy: manager 2 in blue and manager 17 in orange.

figures.caption: Every directed pair of managers sorted by the layers it belongs to. Most tied pairs live in a single layer; only a few are tied in all three.
figures.alt: Horizontal bars, one for each combination of layers. advice: 122. friendship: 41. reporting: 0. advice + friendship: 49. advice + reporting: 8. friendship + reporting: 1. advice + friendship + reporting: 11. A note under the bars says 188 of the 420 directed pairs are tied in no layer.

figures.caption: Each dot is a manager. The horizontal position is the manager's betweenness rank among the advice ties and the vertical position is the rank among the friendship ties (1 is the most between). Manager 17 (orange) is first in friendship and far down in advice. Tied managers share an average rank.
figures.alt: A square scatter plot with 21 dots and a dashed diagonal. The other 20 dots are blue. The orange dot for manager 17 sits at the top of the plot, rank 1 on the friendship axis, and at rank 16 of 21 on the advice axis, far from the diagonal.

figures.caption: Correlations between ten layers among Sampson's 18 novices: liking at three times, esteem, praise and positive influence, then their negative counterparts. The positive relations other than liking go together, the negative ones go together, and liking stands apart from both.
figures.alt: A ten by ten grid of numbers shaded blue for positive and red for negative correlations. The three liking rows form a blue block with values from 0.54 to 0.64. Esteem, praise and positive influence form a second blue block from 0.54 to 0.67. The four negative relations form a third blue block from 0.28 to 0.65. Between the second and third blocks every value is red, from -0.22 to -0.12. Liking at time 3 against esteem is only 0.07.

figures.caption: Seven pairs of layers, three from Krackhardt's managers and four from Sampson's novices. The blue bar is the Jaccard index, the dashed box is the highest it could be for those layer sizes and the orange tick is the value if ties were scattered independently. Advice and reporting sit almost at their ceiling; liking at time 3 with esteem or disliking sits close to the orange tick.
figures.alt: Seven rows, each with a blue bar, a dashed box and an orange tick. advice & friendship: observed 0.26, ceiling 0.54, by luck 0.19. advice & reports to: observed 0.10, ceiling 0.11, by luck 0.05. friendship & reports to: observed 0.11, ceiling 0.20, by luck 0.04. liking t1 & liking t2: observed 0.45, ceiling 0.96, by luck 0.10. liking t2 & liking t3: observed 0.55, ceiling 0.98, by luck 0.10. liking t3 & esteem: observed 0.13, ceiling 0.96, by luck 0.10. liking t3 & disliking: observed 0.11, ceiling 0.84, by luck 0.09.

figures.caption: One small network held four ways. Snapshots keep two photographs and lose the order inside each. Aggregation piles contacts into one picture, or looks through a moving window. An event stream keeps every contact and its time. Intervals give each contact a start and an end.
figures.alt: Four panels, each showing the same six contacts among Ana, Ben, Cleo, Dev, Eli and Fay. Panel 1 shows two small networks, times 1 to 3 with three ties and times 4 to 6 with three ties. Panel 2 shows one network of everything up to time 6 with five ties, the Ana-Ben tie drawn thick because they met twice, and a sliding window of times 3 to 5 with three ties. Panel 3 is a timeline with six ticks labeled A-B at 1, C-D at 2, B-C at 3, D-E at 4, A-B at 5 and E-F at 6. Panel 4 shows five rows of pairs with a short bar for each meeting, A-B twice, at times 1 and 5.

figures.caption: Who can reach whom. Left: the six contacts piled into one picture, where everyone is connected to everyone. Right: the same contacts when a message can only move forward in time. Rows are where a message starts, columns where it can arrive.
figures.alt: Two six by six grids with people in rows and columns. The left grid has every off-diagonal cell filled, 30 of 30 pairs. The right grid has 17 of 30 cells filled. Ana's row has Ben and Cleo filled, Ben's row has Ana and Cleo, Cleo's and Dev's rows have all five others, Eli's row has Dev and Fay, and Fay's row has only Eli.

figures.caption: Sampson's liking choices among 18 novices at times 1, 2 and 3, drawn in the same places each time. Dot size shows how many novices chose that person at that time. The three most chosen at each time are filled and named.
figures.alt: Three copies of the same 18 dots joined by arrows, with 55 arrows at time 1, 57 at time 2 and 56 at time 3. Filled dots mark the three most chosen novices. At time 1 they are Romuald, Bonaventure, Albert. At time 2 they are Bonaventure, Romuald, Peter. At time 3 they are Bonaventure, Boniface, Peter.

figures.caption: How many of the 56 ordered pairs of coworkers can reach each other within the first 48 hours, for the real log (orange) and for 79 versions in which the same timestamps are dealt out to the pairs from a different starting point. The real log sits inside the spread.
figures.alt: A bar chart. The horizontal axis is the number of the 56 ordered pairs that can reach each other, from 17 to 34. Bar heights count how many of 79 shifted logs give that number, with the tallest bar for 17 shifts. The real log, at 28 pairs, is drawn in orange; 8 of the 79 shifted logs reach 28 pairs or more.

figures.caption: The 177 country units of Natural Earth as a spatial network. A dot is a unit's label point and a line is a shared land border; the longest lines are the two orange dashed ones, which come from French Guiana.
figures.alt: A flat world map. Blue dots mark countries and blue lines join neighbouring countries, forming a connected web across Europe, Africa, Asia and South America, with a looser set of ties in North and Central America. Hollow dots are islands with no land border. Two orange dashed lines run from the dot for France, at Paris, across the Atlantic to the dots for Brazil and Suriname.

figures.caption: Share of country pairs that share a land border, by the distance between their label points. Ties are common among close pairs and rare among distant ones, but the 3000 km and beyond bin is not zero.
figures.alt: A bar chart with seven bars. The share of pairs with a shared border is 65.8 percent, 31.2 percent, 14.0 percent, 4.4 percent, 1.2 percent, 1.5 percent, and 0.1 percent for the bins 0 to 500, 500 to 1000, 1000 to 1500, 1500 to 2000, 2000 to 2500, 2500 to 3000 and 3000 kilometres and more. The bars fall steeply from left to right, then flatten near zero.

figures.caption: The same 177 label points joined by distance alone, at three radii. A small radius misses most real borders and leaves most units alone; a large one joins whole regions into one dense knot.
figures.alt: Three side-by-side world maps with dots at the country label points. The first, within 500 kilometres, has 149 lines of which 98 are real borders. The second, within 1000 kilometres, has 470 lines of which 198 are real borders. The third, within 2000 kilometres, has 1475 lines of which 287 are real borders. Real borders are drawn in blue and the rest in grey; the third map has many grey lines, most of all in Europe.

figures.caption: Menger's theorem on six people. The blue route (s, a, b, t) and the orange route (s, d, c, t) share nobody in between, so at least two people must be removed to separate s from t. Removing a and d (dashed rings) does separate them, so two is exactly the number.
figures.alt: Six circles on a hexagon labeled s, a, b, t, c and d, joined in a ring, plus a grey line between a and c across the middle. The ring path s, a, b, t is drawn thick blue and the ring path s, d, c, t is drawn thick orange. The circles a and d have dashed rings around them.

figures.caption: The Florentine marriage network with its 4 cut points (orange squares) and 5 bridges (dashed marriages). Every bridge leads to a family with a single marriage or to a pair that hangs off one.
figures.alt: The fifteen-family marriage network. Four families are drawn as orange squares: Medici, Albizzi, Guadagni, Salviati. Five marriages are drawn as thick dashed lines: Acciaiuoli–Medici; Albizzi–Ginori; Guadagni–Lamberteschi; Medici–Salviati; Pazzi–Salviati. All other families are blue circles and the other marriages are thin grey lines.

figures.caption: Remove each family in turn and count the families in the largest piece that is left. Four families (orange) split the network; the Medici's removal leaves pieces of 11, 2 and 1.
figures.alt: A bar for each of the fifteen families, sorted from shortest to longest. The shortest bar is for the Medici at 11. Albizzi, Guadagni and Salviati have bars of 13. All eleven other bars reach 14. The four shorter bars are orange and the rest blue.

figures.caption: Density is mean degree divided by n - 1. Hold the number of ties per person fixed and density falls toward zero as the network grows. The circles mark the rings of 20, 100 and 500 people from the code.
figures.alt: A chart with the number of people from 10 to 10,000 on a log scale across the bottom and density from 0 to 1 up the side. Two curves fall steeply and then flatten near zero: one for everyone having 4 ties, one for 10 ties. Three circles on the 4-tie curve mark 20 people at 0.211, 100 people at 0.040 and 500 people at 0.008.

figures.caption: Mean distance in 1,000 random networks that keep every node's number of ties, for the Florentine marriages and Krackhardt's friendships. In both, the real mean distance sits in the middle of the shuffled values, so it follows from the degrees. The draws behind this picture are not the ones in the code, so the counts differ slightly.
figures.alt: Two histograms, one above the other. Top: Florentine marriages, with an orange line at the real mean distance 2.486 near the middle of a spread whose average is 2.52; 119 of 1,000 shuffles were disconnected. Bottom: Krackhardt friendships, with the real value 1.648 near the middle of a narrow spread whose average is 1.648; none of the shuffles was disconnected.

figures.caption: The triad census of the advice network (bars) against random networks that keep the dyad census (orange) and random networks that keep every manager's in- and out-degree (purple). Each band holds the central 95 percent of 1,000 draws. The transitive pecking order 030T looks heavily over-represented against the first and ordinary against the second.
figures.alt: A horizontal bar chart with one row for each of the 16 triad types. Observed counts range from 2 (030C) to 190 (030T). Two short bands sit on each bar, the central 95 percent of random networks. For 030T the observed count of 190 is above the band of networks that keep the dyad census (92 to 124) and inside the band of networks that keep every in- and out-degree (184 to 283).

figures.caption: A triangle with a tail. Chloe has three friends but only one of her three pairs of friends is tied, so her local coefficient is 0.33. The global ratio and the two averages of the local coefficients give three different numbers for the same network.
figures.alt: Five people drawn as dots. Ana, Ben and Chloe form a triangle. Dev is tied to Chloe and Eli is tied to Dev. Local clustering is 1.00 for Ana, 1.00 for Ben, 0.33 for Chloe, 0.00 for Dev and undefined for Eli, who has one friend. Beside the picture: global transitivity 0.500, average local clustering 0.583 with Eli left out and 0.467 with Eli counted as zero.

figures.caption: Krackhardt's advice network as a grid. A cell in row i and column j means manager i goes to manager j for advice. Managers are ordered by how many come to them, so the most-asked managers are at the left. Blue cells are returned; orange cells are not.
figures.alt: A 21 by 21 grid with 190 filled cells. 90 are blue, which is 45 returned pairs counted from both sides, and 100 are orange, advice that is not returned. The three most-asked managers, in order, are 2, 18 and 21, and the columns at the left of the grid are the densest.

figures.caption: Three ways to arrange arrows among three people. A transitive triad has a top and a bottom. A cyclic triad has neither. A chain leaves its ends unconnected.
figures.alt: Three triangles of lettered dots with arrows. Left: A points to B, A points to C and B points to C, labeled transitive 030T. Middle: A points to B, B points to C and C points to A, labeled cyclic 030C. Right: A points to B and B points to C, with no arrow between A and C, labeled chain 021C.

figures.caption: The four triangles a signed network can contain. Balanced triangles have an even number of negative ties (none or two); unbalanced ones have an odd number (one or three). Solid blue lines are positive ties and dashed red lines are negative ones.
figures.alt: Four triangles side by side. The first has three positive ties and is labeled balanced. The second has two positive ties and one negative tie and is labeled unbalanced. The third has one positive tie and two negative ties and is labeled balanced. The fourth has three negative ties and is labeled unbalanced.

figures.caption: Sampson's novices at time 3: positive ties (liking, solid blue) and negative ties (disliking, dashed red), drawn only where every choice about the pair had the same sign. The novices are split into the two camps that leave the fewest ties disagreeing; those ties are drawn thick.
figures.alt: A network of 18 named novices joined by 55 ties, 29 positive and 26 negative. Eleven novices are drawn as open circles and seven as filled squares. 11 ties disagree with that split: 8 negative ties inside a camp and 3 positive ties between the camps.

figures.caption: The same 34 karate club members with ties kept only if Zachary saw the pair in at least 1, 3 or 5 kinds of situation. Line thickness shows how many. Filled orange dots have the most ties left; grey dots have none.
figures.alt: Three drawings of the same 34 dots. With every tie kept there are 78 ties in 1 piece. Keeping ties seen in at least 3 contexts leaves 48 ties in 7 pieces. Keeping at least 5 leaves 9 ties in 25 pieces, most dots with no tie at all.

figures.caption: The six-person office used for the hand-worked numbers. Floor 1 (blue circles) has four people, floor 2 (orange squares) has two. Five of the seven ties stay within a floor.
figures.alt: Six labelled nodes. Ana, Ben, Chloe and Dev are blue circles; Eli and Fay are orange squares. Solid grey lines join Ana, Ben and Chloe in a triangle, Chloe to Dev, and Eli to Fay. Dashed red lines join Dev to Eli and Ben to Fay, the only two ties that cross between floors.

figures.caption: Zachary's karate club, coloured by the side each member took when the club split. Most ties (grey) stay on one side; eleven (dashed red) cross.
figures.alt: A network of 34 nodes in two loose clusters. One cluster of 17 blue circles and one of 17 orange squares. Grey lines run mostly inside each cluster; 11 dashed red lines run between the clusters.

figures.caption: Esteem choices among Sampson's novices, counted by the group of the chooser (rows) and the group chosen (columns). The left table is observed. The right table is what the same row and column totals would give if choices ignored groups. The diagonal is where homophily shows.
figures.alt: Two side-by-side four by four tables with rows and columns Turks, Loyal, Outcasts and Waverers. In the left table the diagonal cells hold 20, 10, 6 and 0 and are the darkest. In the right table the diagonal cells hold 11.1, 4.1, 1.2 and 0.7, and no cell is much darker than the others.

figures.caption: Newman's assortativity coefficient for the karate faction labels, shuffled 5,000 times over the same network, against the real value of 0.718. Shuffling keeps the group sizes and the ties and breaks only the link between a person and a label. The draws behind this picture are not the ones in the code, so counts differ slightly.
figures.alt: A histogram centred a little below zero, running from about -0.3 to 0.4, with a peak near -0.05. A black vertical line at 0.718 sits far to the right of every bar. The shuffled values average -0.053 and the largest is 0.384.

figures.caption: Why pairs are not independent observations. One ordered pair (blue) and every pair that shares a person with it (orange), among seven people. Each person appears in many pairs, so what is true of that person is true of all of them at once.
figures.alt: A seven by seven grid with people in rows and columns. The cell in row Cleo, column Eli is blue. 21 other off-diagonal cells are orange: all those in the rows and columns of Cleo and of Eli. The remaining 20 off-diagonal cells are white. Text beside the grid says that among 21 managers each pair shares a person with 77 of the other 419 pairs.

figures.caption: The reference distribution of the level-gap t statistic for the advice network, from 1,000 relabelings of the managers by double semi-partialling. The dashed lines are the cutoffs an ordinary test would use. The observed value sits well outside them and well inside the relabeled distribution.
figures.alt: A histogram of 1,000 relabeled t statistics for the level gap, centered near zero and spread from about -7.4 to 7.6. Dashed vertical lines mark plus and minus 1.97, the ordinary test cutoffs. A solid line marks the observed t of 2.72. Bars at least that far from zero are orange and hold 27% of the draws. The 95th percentile of the absolute relabeled t is 4.93.

figures.caption: Standardized coefficients for advice with the ordinary 95% interval (blue line) and the band that 95% of relabeled coefficients fall in (gray). Where the line is much shorter than the band, the ordinary test is overconfident. A filled dot lies outside the band.
figures.alt: Six rows, one per predictor, each with a gray band, a blue horizontal line and a dot. The dot is outside the gray band, and filled, only for reports_to. The blue line, the ordinary interval, stays on one side of zero for friendship, reports_to, level_gap, tenure_gap. For all but the filled dots the dot is hollow and inside the band.

figures.caption: The 34 members of the karate club. Left: most members have few ties and a handful have many. Right: the same distribution as a complementary cumulative distribution on log axes, the form used to look at tails.
figures.alt: Two charts of karate club degrees. The bar chart shows 11 members with 2 ties, 6 with 3, 6 with 4, one with 1 tie, and single members with 9, 10, 12, 16 and 17 ties. The log-log chart plots the share of members with at least k ties; it starts at 1 for k = 1 and falls to 0.029 at k = 17.

figures.caption: Complementary cumulative degree distributions of two networks of 2,000 people with the same average degree. The random network's tail falls away steeply after about ten ties; the grown network's tail stretches to well over a hundred.
figures.alt: A log-log plot with two clouds of dots. The orange squares, a network with ties placed at random, run from share 1 at degree 1 and drop sharply, ending at degree 13. The blue circles, a network grown by preferential attachment, fall in a nearly straight slope and end at degree 110.

figures.caption: Rewiring a ring lattice. A few rewired ties collapse the mean distance while clustering barely moves; clustering falls only when a large share of ties has been rewired. The small-world range is the stretch in between.
figures.alt: A line chart with a log horizontal axis from 0.0001 to 1. The solid blue line, clustering relative to the ring, stays near 1 until about p = 0.03 and then falls to 0.01 at p = 1. The dashed orange line, mean distance relative to the ring, drops early: it is 0.18 at p = 0.01, while clustering there is still 0.97, and it ends at 0.07.

figures.caption: Each network against two random baselines. The left panel is how clustered the network is; the right is how far apart people are. Keeping every person's degree (blue) usually moves the random baseline toward the observed network, so it is the harder one to beat.
figures.alt: Two panels with three groups of three dots each, one group per network: karate, florentine and managers. Each group shows the observed value in black, the random-ties baseline in orange and the same-degrees baseline in blue. karate transitivity: observed 0.26, random 0.14, same degrees 0.23. florentine transitivity: observed 0.19, random 0.17, same degrees 0.16. managers transitivity: observed 0.47, random 0.37, same degrees 0.46. karate mean distance: observed 2.41, random 2.40, same degrees 2.25. florentine mean distance: observed 2.49, random 2.43, same degrees 2.51. managers mean distance: observed 1.65, random 1.65, same degrees 1.65.

figures.caption: Simple contagion (SI, infection chance 0.2 per tie per step) on the karate club, 1,500 simulated outbreaks per seed rule. Lines are the average number of members infected; shaded bands hold the middle 95 percent of runs. The dotted line marks half the club. The outbreak is simulated; only the ties are observed.
figures.alt: Three rising curves of the number of karate club members infected over 16 steps, each starting at 1. By step 16 the average is 33.8, 33.3 and 30.7 for the best-connected, random and one-tie seeds. The average passes half the club (17) at step 4 for the best-connected seed, step 6 for the random seed and step 8 for the one-tie seed. Shaded bands around each line show the middle 95 percent of runs; the widest band is 33 members tall, for the seed 'seeded at the member with one tie'.

figures.caption: Average share of the karate club that ends up infected after one random seed, against the transmissibility T (SIR, 1,000 simulated outbreaks per value). The shaded band holds the middle 95 percent of runs. The dashed line is the degree-moment threshold. With 34 people the curve bends gradually; it does not jump at the threshold.
figures.alt: A curve rising from about 0.03 at T = 0.025 to about 0.85 at T = 0.6, with a dashed vertical line at T = 0.148. The average share infected is 0.24 at T = 0.25 and 0.69 at T = 0.5. The lower edge of the shaded band stays at one person out of 34 (the seed alone) for every T up to 0.600, because some outbreaks die at once.

figures.caption: Share of a 60-person network that has adopted, by step, averaged over 500 simulated runs per line, from one random member plus two of their contacts. Left: each contact passes it on with chance 0.15 per step. Right: a person adopts once two of their contacts have. The clustered ring is a 60-person ring where each person is tied to the three people on either side; the rewired network re-draws every tie's far end at random.
figures.alt: Two panels of rising curves. On the left, simple contagion has reached 0.98 of the clustered ring (solid) and 1.00 of the rewired network (dashed) by step 30; at step 8 the figures are 0.32 and 0.80. On the right, complex contagion has reached 1.00 of the clustered ring by step 30 and 0.41 of the rewired network.

figures.caption: Mean area under the ROC curve (with one standard deviation across splits) and mean precision at k for eleven scores on 100 splits of the karate club, 20 percent of the ties hidden each time. The dashed line is chance.
figures.alt: Two panels listing eleven scores from common neighbours down to a six-dimension embedding. In the left panel the dots for the mean area under the curve lie between 0.60 and 0.75, every one to the right of the dashed chance line at 0.5, and each has a horizontal bar about 0.05 to 0.08 long on either side. The highest dot is the embedding, 3 dims at 0.751. In the right panel the dots for precision at k lie between 0.01 and 0.24, all to the right of the dashed chance line at 0.032 except Jaccard, which lies to its left.

figures.caption: The karate club placed by two eigenvectors of its normalised Laplacian, coloured by the side each member took. One coordinate nearly separates the two sides.
figures.alt: A scatter plot of 34 points. Blue circles for the 17 members on Mr. Hi's side and orange squares for the 17 members on the officer's side, separated by a dashed vertical line, with the circles mostly on one side of it and the squares on the other. 2 points lie on the wrong side of the line: members 3, 9.

figures.caption: Dropping a random tenth of the advice ties 200 times. Each dot is a manager's score in the full network and each bar spans the middle 90 percent of the scores across the 200 drops.
figures.alt: Two panels, each listing six managers. Left, betweenness: manager 18 has the highest dot at 88.9 with a bar from 73.8 to 107.6; the next dot, manager 21, is at 60.1 with a bar from 43.3 to 80.9. Right, number of people who asked each manager for advice: manager 2 has the highest dot at 18 with a bar from 14.0 to 18.0.

figures.caption: Sampson's liking choices at times 1, 2 and 3, drawn in the same places each time. Shape and colour give Sampson's group; filled marks are the three most chosen novices that time; dark lines join mutual pairs and grey arrows are one-way choices.
figures.alt: Three copies of the same 18 marks, one per time, joined by lines and arrows. The marks are circles for the Turks, squares for the Loyal, diamonds for the Outcasts and triangles for the Waverers. Time 1 shows 55 choices with 14 mutual pairs, time 2 shows 57 with 15, time 3 shows 56 with 15. Filled marks are the three most chosen: Romuald, Bonaventure, Albert at time 1, Romuald, Bonaventure, Peter at time 2 and Bonaventure, Peter, Boniface at time 3.

figures.caption: How well the communities of liking at each time (Louvain, seed 1) and Sampson's groups agree, as the adjusted Rand index. The communities of one wave resemble those of the next; none of them resembles Sampson's groups much. The orange frame marks the comparison with the groups.
figures.alt: A four by four grid of numbers with rows and columns Liking time 1, Liking time 2, Liking time 3 and Sampson's groups. The diagonal is 1.00. Liking time 1 and time 2 score 0.45, time 2 and time 3 score 0.85, and time 1 and time 3 score 0.56. Against Sampson's groups the three times score 0.04, 0.17 and 0.08. Cells with higher values are darker blue.

figures.caption: The karate club drawn four times with the same layout. Shape shows the side each member took. In the three method panels, colour shows the group the method found and a heavy black outline marks a member the method puts on the wrong side (a member counts as wrong when most of their group took the other side). Member 9 is wrong in every panel.
figures.alt: Four network pictures of 34 members. Top left, the real split: circles for Mr. Hi's 17 supporters in blue and squares for the officer's 17 in orange, with 11 dashed ties crossing between them. Top right, Louvain finds four colour groups and heavy black outlines mark members 9 and 10. Bottom left, a Fiedler spectral cut finds two groups and heavy black outlines mark members 3 and 9. Bottom right, Zachary's minimum cut finds two groups and a heavy black outline marks only member 9.

figures.caption: Members that each of eleven methods puts on the wrong side. Member 9 is wrong for all eleven, member 10 for four and member 3 for three. Every other member is right for every method.
figures.alt: A grid of eleven methods by three members (3, 9 and 10). A dot means the method misclassifies that member. Member 9 has a dot in every row, 11 of 11. Member 10 has 4 dots and member 3 has 3.

figures.caption: Modularity of the real two-way split (0.358) against 2,000 shuffles of the sides over the real ties and 500 rewirings of the ties that keep every member's degree. The draws behind this picture are not the ones in the code, so the numbers differ slightly.
figures.alt: Two overlapping histograms of modularity, both centred a little below zero and running from about -0.2 to 0.2. A black vertical line at 0.358 lies to the right of every bar. The largest shuffled value is 0.167 and the largest rewired value is 0.102.

figures.caption: One network, two pictures. By number of ties the connector (orange) is the smallest dot in the picture; by betweenness it is the largest, because every route between the two groups runs through it.
figures.alt: Two drawings of the same nine dots: two groups of four dots, each group tied all round, with one dot in the middle tied to one member of each group. On the left, dot size follows the number of ties: the middle dot has 2 ties, the two members it touches have 4 each, and the other six members have 3 each, so the middle dot is the smallest. On the right, dot size follows betweenness: the middle dot is largest at 16, the two members it touches score 15 each, and the other six score 0.

figures.caption: The middle person of a line of n people. The share of shortest routes they sit on settles near one half, while closeness and the degree share both fall toward zero as the line grows.
figures.alt: A line chart against the number of people in the line, from 3 to 101 on a log scale. The betweenness share starts at 1 for 3 people and falls to 0.505 at 101. Closeness falls from 1 at 3 people to 0.039 at 101. The degree share falls from 1 at 3 people to 0.020 at 101.

figures.caption: The weight a tie adds to the GWESP statistic as a function of its number of shared partners, for four decay settings. A tie with no shared partner adds 0 and with one adds exactly 1 whatever the decay. After that each further partner adds less, and the weight levels off at $e^{\alpha}$. The dashed line is the raw count of shared partners.
figures.alt: A line chart with shared partners from 0 to 10 on the horizontal axis and the weight added to GWESP on the vertical axis. Every line starts at 0 for no shared partners and passes through 1 for one shared partner. At 10 shared partners the lines for decay 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 reach 1.28, 1.65, 2.69 and 5.66, and they level off at 1.28, 1.65, 2.72 and 7.39. A dashed straight line shows the raw count, which reaches the top of the chart at 8 shared partners.

figures.caption: Constraint computed from each person's ego network alone, against constraint computed from the whole network. The dashed line is where the two agree. No point lies below it.
figures.alt: Two scatter plots, each with a dashed diagonal. Left, the 21 managers of Krackhardt's firm: whole-network constraint runs from 0.19 to 0.59 and ego-network constraint from 0.20 to 1.12, and 0 of the 21 points lie on the diagonal. Right, the 15 Florentine families: whole-network constraint runs from 0.21 to 1.00 and ego-network constraint from 0.24 to 1.00, and 8 of the 15 points lie on the diagonal. In both plots every other point lies above the diagonal.

figures.caption: The Medici's constraint (orange square) against the lowest constraint among the other families (blue circle), first with the full data and then with each of the Medici's six marriage partners left out in turn.
figures.alt: Seven rows, each with an orange square for the Medici and a blue circle for the family with the lowest constraint among the others. nobody removed: Medici 0.210, Guadagni 0.250; Acciaiuoli removed: Medici 0.262, Guadagni 0.250; Albizzi removed: Medici 0.262, Guadagni 0.333; Barbadori removed: Medici 0.262, Guadagni 0.250; Ridolfi removed: Medici 0.200, Guadagni 0.250; Salviati removed: Medici 0.262, Guadagni 0.250; Tornabuoni removed: Medici 0.200, Albizzi 0.333. The Medici have the lowest constraint in 4 of the 7 rows.

figures.caption: Six people in three positions. People in the top row go to one or both of the middle row, and both in the middle row go to the person at the bottom.
figures.alt: Six circles and squares joined by seven arrows. In the top row, a and b each have arrows to both d and e, and c has one arrow to d. In the middle row, d and e each have an arrow to f, the diamond at the bottom.

figures.caption: The managers' advice table, ordered by four positions from an average-linkage cut of structural-equivalence distances. The blocks are neither empty nor full: this is a rough pattern, not a clean blockmodel. The positions follow level only weakly and department partly.
figures.alt: A 21 by 21 grid of cells, blue where a manager goes to another for advice, with heavy lines dividing the managers into four positions of 9, 8, 2 and 2 managers. On the right, a four by four table of block densities. The two diagonal blocks of the last two positions have densities 1.00 and 1.00, the block from position 3 to position 1 has 0.94, and the block from position 0 to position 1 has 0.04. The densities run from 0.04 to 1.00, so most blocks are neither empty nor full.

figures.caption: Mistakes fall as positions are added, for the real network and for every baseline, so falling alone proves nothing. Shuffling labels (grey) is an easy baseline. Redoing the whole procedure on networks that keep each manager's out-degree (orange and red) is a fair one: the real curve is below its best only from four positions on.
figures.alt: A line chart of mistakes against one to six positions. The real network, a solid blue line, falls from 190 with one position to 120 with two, 90 with four and 76 with six. A grey dashed line for shuffled labels stays well above it. Two lines for networks that keep each manager's out-degree and are clustered again, one for the mean and one for the best of 100 draws, run close to the real line at two and three positions. From four positions on the real line is below the best of the redone draws.

figures.caption: The fitted map of the karate club (large markers) with 40 posterior draws of every member's position (small dots). Each draw was turned and mirrored to match the fitted map, because a map is only defined up to such moves. The cloud around a member shows how far the data let that member's place move.
figures.alt: A scatter of 34 large hollow markers, blue circles for Mr. Hi's side and orange squares for the officer's side, each surrounded by 40 small dots of the same color. The dots lie a root-mean-square 0.8 map units from the fitted position for member 33, the tightest cloud, and 3.8 units for member 18, the widest. The 12 members with at most two friends average 3.3 units, and the 4 members with ten or more friends average 1.0.

figures.caption: Goodness of fit by simulation. For each of three fitted models, 200 networks were simulated and four summaries computed. Bars show the middle 95 percent, dots the median, and the dashed line the karate club's own value. A model fits a summary when the line falls inside its bar.
figures.alt: Four small panels with three horizontal bars each, for the models with the same chance for every pair, the latent space map and hubs and the rest, with a dashed vertical line at the club's value. degree spread (sd): the club's 3.82 lies inside the interval of hubs and the rest; busiest member: the club's 17 lies inside the interval of hubs and the rest; triangles: the club's 45 lies inside the interval of latent space map, hubs and the rest; pairs two steps apart: the club's 265 lies inside the interval of same chance for all, hubs and the rest.

figures.caption: Sampson's novices, liking at three times. Left: between consecutive waves most ties were kept, but many were dropped and many new ones appeared, although the totals barely moved. Right: pooling both steps, the share of ordered pairs of novices that have a tie at the next wave, by whether the tie existed and whether it was returned.
figures.alt: Two panels. On the left, bars for the two steps between waves. From wave 1 to 2: 35 ties kept, 20 dropped and 22 new. From wave 2 to 3: 40 kept, 17 dropped and 16 new. On the right, horizontal bars for the share of ordered pairs with a tie at the next wave: 0.74 (43 of 58) for pairs with a returned tie, 0.59 (32 of 54) for a tie that was not returned, 0.28 (15 of 54) for no tie where the other novice names him, and 0.05 (23 of 446) for no tie either way.

figures.caption: The two event-model coefficients for the eighty invented messages, refitted on each half of the log and with two more effects in the model. Dots are estimates, bars reach two standard errors either side. The halves agree in sign and size, but each half alone is only about two standard errors from zero.
figures.alt: Two panels with four rows each, estimates as dots with bars of two standard errors either side and a dashed line at zero. all 80 messages: inertia -0.75, reply +0.76; first 40: inertia -0.70, reply +0.73; last 40: inertia -0.68, reply +0.63; all 80, plus activity and popularity: inertia -0.68, reply +0.73. In every row the inertia estimate is below zero and the reply estimate is above zero; in the two half-log rows the inertia bars extend slightly past zero and the reply bars begin just above it.

figures.caption: Studying only Mr. Hi's side of the karate club keeps 17 members and 35 ties and cuts 11 ties to members outside the boundary.
figures.alt: A network of 34 numbered members. Seventeen members on Mr. Hi's side are blue circles joined by 35 solid black ties. Seventeen members on the officer's side are faded gray circles joined by faint gray ties. Eleven red dashed ties cross between the two sides.

figures.caption: A two-wave snowball sample from member 12 names 17 members and sees 16 ties. From member 1 it names 26 members and sees 51 ties.
figures.alt: Two drawings of the 34-member karate club. On the left the sample starts at member 12: 17 members are colored, 2 were interviewed, and 16 ties are drawn bold. On the right it starts at member 1: 26 members are colored, 17 were interviewed, and 51 ties are drawn bold. Members never reached are faded gray.

figures.caption: The crisis test on both teams. Remove Ana and her ties. The team where everyone talks to everyone stays in one piece; the hub team falls into four separate people.
figures.alt: Two panels, each with Ana's node faded and drawn with dashed gray lines to the others. On the left, the four remaining people are still joined to each other by six solid lines. On the right, the four remaining people are drawn with no lines between them.

figures.caption: A map of the book. Foundations come first and everything leans on them; describing and modeling are the two big halves; the case studies at the end put the pieces together on real data.
figures.alt: Six labeled boxes in two rows of three, joined by arrows from left to right and a dashed arrow from the end of the first row to the start of the second. Foundations lists four chapters, Describing networks nine, More complex networks five, Modeling networks seven, In practice three and Case studies four.

figures.caption: The three states of a pair of people in a directed network, drawn from the advice network. Ana and Chloe are a mutual dyad; Ana and Ben are asymmetric; Ben and Dev are null. There are ten pairs in all.
figures.alt: The five-person advice network drawn with arrows. The pair Ana and Chloe has arrows in both directions and is labeled mutual. Five pairs, such as Ana and Ben, have an arrow one way and are labeled asymmetric. Four pairs, such as Ben and Dev, have no arrow and are labeled null. A tally box shows 1 mutual, 5 asymmetric and 4 null.

figures.caption: The advice network turned into an undirected one by two rules. Keeping a pair if either person asks gives a connected network of six ties; keeping only mutual pairs leaves a single tie.
figures.alt: Three drawings of the five advice-network people on a circle. Left: the original with seven arrows. Middle: the either rule, with six plain lines and all five people connected. Right: the both rule, with a single line between Ana and Chloe and Ben, Dev and Eli standing alone.

figures.caption: The adjacency matrix of the triangle-with-a-tail network and its square. A shaded cell is a one; the number in each cell of the second grid counts the walks of length two between that pair. The diagonal of the second grid repeats the degrees.
figures.alt: Left: a five by five grid for Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev and Eli with ten shaded cells, symmetric across the diagonal, drawn beside a small network of a triangle with a two-person tail. Right: a five by five grid of numbers whose diagonal reads 2, 2, 3, 2, 1 and whose other entries are 0 or 1.

figures.caption: The same weighted network at three cutoffs. Line thickness shows the number of messages. Raising the cutoff turns a connected network into a hub around Ben and then into a single pair.
figures.alt: Three drawings of the same five people. With every tie kept, six lines join them and Ana and Ben are drawn with a thick line. With a cutoff of two, three lines remain and Ben is joined to Ana, Chloe and Dev while Eli stands alone. With a cutoff of seven, only the Ana and Ben line remains and three people stand alone.

figures.caption: The number of marriages of each of the 15 families, from most to fewest. The Medici stand alone at six; Guadagni and Strozzi follow with four.
figures.alt: A horizontal bar chart of 15 family names. Medici has the longest bar at 6. Guadagni and Strozzi have 4. Six families have 3, Barbadori and Salviati have 2, and four families have 1. A vertical dashed line marks the mean of 2.67.

figures.caption: The three Krackhardt relations by what each pair of managers did. Mutual pairs are returned ties; one-sided pairs are asymmetric. The rule you choose for undirected data (either or both) keeps everything up to the dashed marks, or only the first segment.
figures.alt: Three horizontal bars, one each for advice, friendship and reporting, each split into mutual, one-sided and no-tie pairs out of 210. Advice: 45 mutual, 100 one-sided, 65 none. Friendship: 23, 56, 131. Reporting: 0, 20, 190.

figures.caption: Thresholding the karate club's valued ties. Each step up in the number of shared settings removes ties, and between 2 and 3 the club breaks from one piece into seven.
figures.alt: Two line charts with the threshold, from 1 to 6 shared settings, across the bottom. The first shows ties kept, falling from 78 to 72, 48, 21, 9 and 2. The second shows separate pieces: 1, 1, 7, 19, 25 and 32, with the steepest rise between thresholds 2 and 3.

figures.caption: A file with one lower-case name and one trailing space has seven names for five people. The two phantom nodes (outlined in red) carry the ties that belong to Ana and Chloe.
figures.alt: A drawing with five blue people, Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev and Eli, around a ring, plus two orange nodes outside it, labeled ana and Chloe with a space mark. Two dashed red arrows run from the orange nodes: ana to Chloe and Chloe-space to Ana. To the right, the seven lines of the file and a note that there are seven different strings but five people on the roster.

figures.caption: The tidy form of network data is two tables, one row per node and one row per tie. The adjacency matrix and the adjacency list are views of the tie table.
figures.alt: Left, a table of five people with a team column. Middle, a table of seven ties with source, target and relation columns. Right, an arrow to a five by five matrix of ones and zeros and a list of who each person goes to, labeled as views, not the data.
